questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: My primary motivation in choosing Tokyo as my destination was a personal interest in the destination. I wanted to improve my Japanese, to spend time with friends in Japan, and to get to know the country better. Additionally, University of Tokyo is a very famous and well regarded university in Japan. I was curious to experience what studying there would be like.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had a great semester in Japan, and for anyone who is considering I would say: Go! You won't regret it. No matter what your experience is, I'm certain you will learn a lot and have many fun and memorable experiences.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I found the arrival procedure quite confusing (as well as the visa application process prior to arriving). UTokyo however were great at helping and my contacts there answered all my (many) questions and helped me out when needed.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had a tutor assigned who went to the ward office with me and helped me register for classes etc. I could also ask the international student advisor at my graduate school any questions that my tutor couldn't help with. Because I stayed in a university dorm, I also had support from the dorm in the form of various guides on how to do things, e.g. go to the ward office to register my address and pay my first rent.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I was satisfied, no additional comments.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I applied through the university and was assigned housing. It wasn't complicated, and I was really happy with my choice.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: When I say off campus, the dorm was really right next to one of the campuses, but not the campus I had classes in. Because I didn't live on or close to my campus, I had a 1 hour commute back and forth 4 days a week. It may sound like a lot, but in Tokyo this is completely normal. I usually read a book on the train. The commuter pass also definitely makes sense then if you have classes more than a few days a week.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was very happy with my housing situation. It was conveniently located, cheap, and just a great area to call home for the duration of my stay. It was also a great place to meet other international students, the staff were helpful, and there was a gym nearby that I used a lot.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I found it confusing, but the international student advisor and my tutor helped me understand the process and fill everything out correctly.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: We had an orientation for international students at my graduate school where we received practical information, student ID, and we also were each assigned a desk in a private reading room.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I was assigned a tutor to help with course registration etc. The international student advisor also answered any questions my tutor couldn't. Additionally, my supervisor, a professor in my graduate school, was great. He showed me around campus and seemed to really take an interest in helping me make the most of my time at UTokyo. Generally, I had a lot of support at Utokyo.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I registered for all the classes I wanted, and I was happy with my choices. However there were some courses marked with both Japanese and English, and it was my understanding that I couldn't take those classes with my limited Japanese abilities, but several other students did – so something to watch out for when you choose classes, although it says both Japanese and English you may be able to take the class with only English abilities. If you're unsure, ask the professor.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Look through the course catalogue and don't be afraid to take classes which may not initially sound like they're for you (one of my courses, Anglo-American Law (Special Study), had a description entirely in Japanese which made me think it was mostly aimed at Japanese students, but actually all classes were held in English, and the professors were American). Use the initial period to try out different classes and get an impression of the professors and the workload. Ask the professor if you have any questions.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was very satisfied. Although I didn't particularly learn anything I can use directly at home, I found all my classes interesting, different, and I really enjoyed the opportunity to learn something new. The professors were all great. As a bonus, University of Tokyo is a very important institution in Japan, so it was interesting e.g. to hear about how the university had been tied up in important events in Japanese history.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Because the examination form is quite different from what I'm used to at UCPH, I don't think it really makes sense to compare the level. For most classes I was evaluated based on a final paper or several papers turned in during the course of the semester. It wasn't particularly difficult, but because it was so different from what I'm used to at home I ended up probably spending more time and energy than needed on my assignments.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: All my classes at UTokyo were seminar based, and the classes were generally small compared to what I'm used to from home. The professors seemed to have quite a bit of freedom in how to arrange their classes and evaluate students, so for example the length, form etc. of papers would differ depending on the professor/class. My impression was that the Japanese classes were more lecture based and had written examinations more like those I'm used to at home, so perhaps the differences in teaching style were also related to my taking classes in English.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Anglo-American Law (Special Study)
Sociology of Law (Special Study) / Japanese Law as Viewed from Abroad
Comparative Law (Special Study) / Law and the Formation of Transnational East Asia
Oriental Legal History (Special Study) / Law and Society in East Asia
Japanese Intermediate-2 Speaking
Japanese Intermediate-2 Integral

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I really enjoyed Japanese Law as Viewed from Abroad with Professor Foote. The class provided a great introduction to various areas of Japanese law, to comparative studies more generally, and as most students in class were domestic students in the professional law school program, I also had an opportunity to learn more about them and the legal profession in Japan which was really interesting. Law and the Formation of Transnational East Asia proved to be another (surprising) favorite class. Two professors teach this class together which made the dynamic more interesting than if it had just been one person talking. The subject matter is unlike anything I've learned before but really interesting. Lastly, in Anglo-American Law (Special Study) I thought Professor Sarah Cleveland was brilliant, although I think the visiting professors in this course change from semester to semester, so you should check the course catalogue to see who is teaching.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I didn't encounter any unexpected costs. I was however surprised how inconvenient it was to pay my bills. At first I thought I would have to get a Japanese credit card. I ended up paying my rent by taking out cash each month and then transferring it at the bank. The dorm gave us a guide for this, so it's not that it was very difficult to figure out, I just found it odd that there wasn't an easier way to do it.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Living in Japan generally proved to be quite inexpensive. Food and drink is cheap, transportation can add up but I had a commuter pass so that helped. My biggest expense ended up being travelling which I did a lot of (I've put this in the category "Personal spending"). There are definitely opportunities to travel cheaply, e.g. using highway busses and chain hotels, but I ended up often opting for the comfort and speed of flying or taking the shinkansen which of course was then more expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't participate in any clubs or circles. From the people I know who did, I think it's a great opportunity, especially if you want to make friends with local students. It seemed to be mostly aimed at undergraduate students though.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I took Japanese language classes through JLCSE. They also held some cultural events. I participated in a calligraphy class, and there was also e.g. a kimono wearing event. I think there's probably more activities at Komaba campus where all the undergraduate students have their classes than there are at Hongo. Of course if you join a club or circle they'll have more offers. There was a student festival at Hongo campus in May. There's also a gym in Hongo, I didn't use it but heard good things about it from those who did.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: If you have an interest in any sports or crafts, and if you want to make friends with local students, clubs or circles seem to be a great way to do so. If not, there are also plenty of other ways to meet people. Living at the dorm, someone was always going on some trip or doing something, so there were plenty of opportunities to participate in things.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Tokyo is a great city to live in. There's always something going on and you'll never be bored. However, it can also be crowded and tiring, so on weekends and holidays I would recommend travelling around Japan and especially seeing more of the countryside. There were so many places I enjoyed seeing on day- or longer trips. Just some highlights: the Izu peninsula is great and not so far from Tokyo, Karuizawa I really liked as well, if you enjoy hiking there's many hiking opportunities close to Tokyo, e.g. Mt Mitake, Mt Tsukuba, Mt Nokogiri, the Jogasaki coast, as well as longer hikes further from Tokyo such as the Kiso Road, Mt Fuji etc. I also travelled to further away places such as Hokkaido, Shikoku and Kyushu. Flight tickets are pretty cheap, and being in Japan for a longer time is a great opportunity to see those places you wouldn't necessarily on vacation. If you're here during the summer don't miss the festivals and fireworks. And if you want to see cherry blossoms, make sure to arrive in March as they bloom earlier and earlier every year – some students who arrived in the beginning of April almost missed the blossoms entirely which was a shame. In general, enjoy the seasons as they come and go – if you're here during the spring, you'll have the rainy season and the hot and humid summer, but you'll also have cherry blossoms, azaleas, and my favorite, the hydrangeas which you can see blooming all over Tokyo in June.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Some things were easier to adjust to than others. Generally though, I didn't find anything particularly difficult. Everything is different but that's part of the experience.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Not really, just be friendly and talk to people. If you take classes in English, usually the Japanese people in those classes will be those who are already comfortable speaking English, so it shouldn't be impossible to talk to them. Generally though, I think the consensus is that while everyone is really friendly it can be hard to make deeper connections with local students. But don't let that scare you. Talk to people and enjoy the opportunity to be surprised and delighted at how different but also similar we all are.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I guess the language barrier was the biggest challenge. Even though I can understand a lot, I often found it difficult to participate in conversations in a natural way.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The convenience and the friendliness. And the food!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Before you leave, there will be lots of paperwork and practical tasks of e.g. applying for your visa and subletting your apartment. These things may make you question why you're bothering to go on exchange at all, but don't worry, it's worth all the trouble. 

2. Everyone else is as confused as you in the beginning. Don't be afraid to ask questions. Japanese people are incredibly friendly and helpful, and even if you make mistakes, don't worry as you can always find a solution.

3. If your classes are at Hongo, enjoy the campus – Sanshiro pond, the library, the gingko trees, the arched hallways. I miss it already.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: There's probably a lot, but I don't remember everything now. You will have a lot of questions and maybe sometimes things will seem difficult, but everything will work out.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Any time I spoke Japanese, was understood, and made connections with people. Any time I felt that I understood the culture and fit in. Just the general joy of making a life for yourself across the world, of eating and travelling and experiencing, and of reflecting on my life at home and understanding it better - both the good and the bad - because of the added outside perspective.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I found being away from family and friends at home difficult. The time difference means that when you wake up, everyone at home is asleep, and when they wake up, you're probably in class or otherwise too busy to talk, then when you get home in the evening they're at work. Dealing with a loss in the family at home while I was abroad was the hardest time during my exchange.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
